messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sarah, a 33-year-old paramedic, still replays the moment in fragments. Eighteen months ago, she responded to a middle-aged man in anaphylactic shock. In the chaos of the back of the rig, she miscalculated the epinephrine dose and injected it into an artery instead of muscle. Within seconds, the man suffered a stroke that left him partially paralyzed. She knows it was her hand that did it—her mistake, her fault. The memory does not come as a story; it comes as a series of snapshots: the man’s terrified eyes, the syringe plunger, the sudden flatline on the monitor. Each piece arrives without warning, and when it does, the same visceral terror she felt that night floods back. She never knows when the next fragment will hit—while she is driving to a call, while she is trying to fall asleep, while she is sitting at the dinner table with her husband.

To hold the terror at bay, Sarah has developed a set of strategies that feel necessary in the moment. When a memory fragment intrudes, she reaches for a drink as soon as she is off shift, or she scrolls through her phone for hours, or she turns the television volume up until the noise drowns the images. She refuses to talk about the event with anyone—not her colleagues, not her husband, not even the mandatory debriefing counselor. What she has not realized is that each time she deliberately pushes the memory away, it seems to come back stronger the next day, as if the act of suppression gives the snapshots more power. The same alcohol that deadens the terror in the evening leaves her restless and on edge the following morning, her heart racing at the smallest unexpected sound.

The terror on recall has also reshaped how she experiences the world as dangerous. She finds herself scanning the ambulance bay for signs of emergency, her eyes darting to every phone that rings, every shout. At night, she is worse. She cannot relax in the dark; she checks the locks on the front door three times, lies awake listening to the house creak, feeling certain that something terrible is about to happen. This hypervigilance, in turn, feeds the memories. When she startles at a sound—a car backfiring, a drawer slamming—her mind immediately jumps to the monitor alarm from that night, and a new snapshot of the man’s face appears. It is a vicious circle: the more she tries to stay alert to prevent another catastrophe, the more she is reminded of the first one.

Her concentration has suffered badly. She finds herself losing track of equipment inventories on the rig, misplacing her radio, failing to follow conversations in the station. This only deepens her conviction that she is a danger to her patients. She has started to avoid certain kinds of calls—anything involving anaphylaxis or epinephrine—and when the dispatcher sends her near the intersection where the incident occurred, her pulse spikes and she has to pull over. Her husband has grown frustrated with her distance and her refusal to explain why she flinches at every mention of work. A month ago, he told her that if she did not get help, he could not continue living like this.

She has finally come to see a therapist, reluctantly, at her husband’s insistence. What she hopes for is to stop the snapshots from coming, or at least to make them less terrifying. What she fears most is that talking about it will bring the full terror back, and that she will lose her career or her marriage. But she is also exhausted from the constant watchfulness and the effort of pretending she is fine. She is willing to try, even though she does not believe it will work.
